channel.title: Signal Digest
channel.description: Two-host digests auto-generated across multiple shows -- Signal Digest (AI: IBM Technology, Y Combinator, Matt Pocock, Silicon Valley Girl) and Longview (geopolitics/economics/history: Economics Explained, Predictive History, Warographics), with more topics planned. Each episode's hosts find the cross-cutting threads in that show's sources.
channel.itunes:author: Signal Digest

item.title: Science: Who's Afraid of the Stars?
item.description: We've weaponized the very language of progress and destiny to surveil our minds, choose our battles, and even hand us artificial versions of truth itself – so who exactly controls the telescope we're peering through? The language of inevitability – whether it's cosmic expansion, empire, or technological progress – is used to justify present actions and disempower alternative futures. Synthesized from DOAC, JRE, StarTalk.

item.title: Science: Preparing for the Unknown: Fear, Psychedelics, and AI
item.description: What if the same fear that keeps us alive is the thing we need to transcend for the next leap in consciousness? Fear can be managed through preparation and exposure, not eliminated, and this principle applies across high-stakes domains like climbing, psychedelic experiences, and AI's existential threats. Synthesized from DOAC, JRE, StarTalk.

item.title: Vital Signs: The Star and the Science: Separating Longevity Gurus from Their Claims
item.description: The most credible longevity advice this week comes from a man in the middle of a credibility crisis, and the harshest critique of a biohacker's diet is the one that may have caused his own autoimmune condition. The messenger is not the message: this week's biggest throughline is the growing split between the personal credibility of longevity influencers (Attia's Epstein fallout, Johnson's health crisis) and the scientific validity of their core protocols, forcing audiences to decouple the brand from the biology.

item.title: Longview: The Hidden Winners and Losing Legacies
item.description: While the world watches the fighting, Russia and China are quietly winning the Iran war—making peace less likely with every passing day. The Iran conflict is creating a strategic incentive alignment for Russia and China to prolong the war, as both gain economic and geopolitical advantages from its continuation, making negotiated peace increasingly difficult. Synthesized from Economics Explained, Predictive History, Warographics.

item.title: The Post-Model Economy: Who Owns the Tollbooth?
item.description: Stripe just paid $7 billion for a company most people have never heard of—because the model isn't the product anymore. The model layer is commoditizing, and the real value is shifting to the orchestration, routing, and control plane that sits above models and beneath the enterprise. Synthesized from IBM Technology, Matt Pocock, Silicon Valley Girl, Y Combinator.

item.title: Science: The Perception Gap: How Our Headsets Shape Reality
item.description: Your brain isn't a window on reality—it's a VR headset, and evolution's price of admission is blindness to the truth. Our evolved cognitive shortcuts make us vulnerable to hijacking by external triggers—whether AI-driven social media algorithms or the psychological manipulation of virality—so our 'reality' can be shaped by forces designed to exploit those shortcuts. Synthesized from DOAC, JRE, StarTalk.

item.title: Vital Signs: The Wake-Up Call: Autoimmune Reality vs. Data-Driven Longevity
item.description: A $2 million-a-year biomarker tracking system missed an autoimmune disease that 'changed everything' for Bryan Johnson—how much does all this data actually tell us? The limits of self-quantification: Bryan Johnson's autoimmune diagnosis, despite his extensive biomarker tracking, exposes the gap between data-driven longevity and real medical reality, prompting a need for humility and integration of clinical symptoms.

item.title: Longview: When Cheap Beats Strong: The New Math of Power
item.description: A single F-16 costs $30 million—and can be replaced by 60,000 cheap drones that don't need a pilot to die. Strategic dominance built on expensive, complex platforms is vulnerable to low-cost asymmetries, whether in drones, economic models, or the confidence of wealthy residents, which enables smaller or poorer actors to shift the balance. Synthesized from Economics Explained, Predictive History, Warographics.

item.title: Longview: The Economic Siege: Iran's War on a Timer
item.description: Iran's military can keep firing $20,000 drones, but its civilians are running out of food, water, and patience. Iran's underlying economic fragility undercuts the cost-asymmetry argument, creating a finite timeline for its war effort. Synthesized from Economics Explained, Predictive History, Warographics.

item.title: The Containment Paradox: Open Models, Closed Gaps, and the Security Tightrope
item.description: When your own AI gets hacked and you delay the next release, the real headline isn't the model—it's the uncomfortable truth that keeping secrets might be the only way to keep control. The open vs. closed model debate is a security tension, not just an ideological one: while open models democratize access and accelerate innovation, they also spread capabilities that can be weaponized, forcing organizations to balance openness against containment. Synthesized from IBM Technology, Y Combinator.

item.title: Architect Prep: Scenario walkthroughs — all six bank scenarios end-to-end, plus exam-day strategy
item.description: A misconfigured `always_ask` on your bash tool can stall your entire customer-support session like that, but get the debug CI backoff wrong and you'll watch your multi-agent orchestration burn tokens three-times over—today we break down the six scenarios you'll most likely see on the exam. Customer Support Resolution Agent — full scenario walkthrough with the architecture decision points Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 5 — subagent isolation, scratchpads, stateless Messages API design, confidence-based escalation
item.description: The Messages API forgets nothing—but it never remembers anything either: so who's responsible when your customer-support agent loses the ticket context mid-escalation? Subagent isolation — what it buys you and what it costs, and when to pay for it Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 2 — tool design, structured tool errors, MCP scopes & authentication, tool_choice
item.description: Your tool description is the difference between Claude calling get_weather or hallucinating a weather report—so why is yours still one sentence? Writing a high-quality tool description — what makes the model pick the right tool reliably Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 4 — the reliability ladder for structured output, JSON-schema tool use, and fabrication prevention
item.description: Without strict schema constraints, Claude might return `passengers: "two"` — and your booking system crashes. Here's how to climb the reliability ladder from free-text to schema-constrained tool use. The reliability ladder: free-text → formatted prose → JSON-mode → schema-constrained tool use Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 3b — slash commands & Skills, plan mode, iterative refinement, configuration trade-offs
item.description: Your CLAUDE.md is bloated and every word you add to it costs tokens on every single session — but a Skill's 100-token description is free until you actually need the procedure. Custom slash commands vs Skills — when a procedure should become one or the other Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 3a — CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/, settings, and permissions
item.description: A deny rule in your settings blocks `Bash(aws *)` — but your Claude.md says 'never deploy to prod' — which one actually enforces the policy when Claude reaches for the AWS CLI? What belongs in CLAUDE.md vs what belongs in .claude/rules/ Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 1b — PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, stop_reason loop control, session resumption, resolution vs escalation
item.description: A PostToolUse hook can enforce what a system prompt never can — it auto-runs Prettier after every Edit, so 'format this file' isn't a request, it's a guarantee. PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks — what each can enforce that a system prompt cannot Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Orientation — how the Claude Certified Architect exam actually works
item.description: The exam won't ask you to recite what an MCP server is—it'll hand you a scenario where a single agent with every skill is choking on context, and all four wrong answers sound like the right tool until you realize they've slipped a subagent into a thread that has 20-agent roster limits. What the exam is actually testing: architectural judgment on scenarios, not trivia recall Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Architect Prep: Domain 1a — orchestration-layer safeguards, structured handoffs, dynamic task decomposition
item.description: When you delegate to a subagent, the only thing that crosses the boundary is the prompt string you pass to the Agent tool -- not your system prompt, not your conversation history, not your secrets. Choosing orchestration-layer safeguards (hooks, permission policies, tool restrictions) vs relying on model judgment inside a single agent -- the model-discretion trap Synthesized from Anthropic docs.

item.title: Science: The Attention Economy of AI
item.description: AI is engineering human desire, and the only way to fight it is with critical thinking. AI's capacity to exploit human psychology for engagement poses a threat to individual and societal well-being, as seen in its ability to generate misinformation and create addictive social interactions. Synthesized from DOAC, JRE, StarTalk.

item.title: Karpathy: The Jagged Frontier: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
item.description: I don't think I've typed a line of code since December — and I've never felt more behind as a programmer. The new bottleneck in AI-driven development is human judgment and understanding, not coding ability, as agents handle increasingly complex tasks while humans must direct them with taste and oversight. Synthesized from No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups, Sequoia Capital.

item.title: The Skill Trap: When Letting AI Cook Means Trusting Strangers
item.description: Over 35% of 4,000 public agent skills have security flaws — one in eight is critical. Agent skills are only as good as the expertise and boundaries encoded into them: the real risk isn't the model's hallucination but the unseen dependencies and untrusted third-party code that a skill can execute, making security and vetting as important as the prompt. Synthesized from IBM Technology, Y Combinator.

item.title: Science: The Uncontainable: AI, Fiction, and Friction
item.description: Containment is not possible, but it has to be possible, because otherwise it contains us. AI's omni-use nature and the paradox of control: the same technology that can find tumors can target battlefield targets, making effective containment both impossible and essential, while competitive pressures drive every organization to race for intelligence regardless of risk. Synthesized from DOAC, JRE, StarTalk.

item.title: Vital Signs: Reprogramming, Rapamycin, and the Credibility Crisis
item.description: This week, the first human was dosed in a trial that could prove age reversal is real—while the man who told you how to live longer just had his credibility explode. The first FDA-cleared in vivo reprogramming trial in humans (Sinclair/Life Biosciences) signals a shift from animal models to human testing, but the science is far from settled: the Rapamycin + exercise RCT shows that even promising drugs can fail to outperform lifestyle, reinforcing that exercise — not any drug — remains the proven foundation for longevity.

item.title: Longview: The Balance Sheet of Empire: Debt, Drones, and the Cost of Stability
item.description: The world's wealth just hit $600 trillion—but three-quarters of it is a mirage, and nearly a third is debt that could explode at any moment. The global economy runs on a fragile fiction: net worth has inflated through asset price bubbles and debt rather than productive investment, so the entire system is exposed to a balance-sheet reckoning that would hit households, states, and strategic rivals alike. Synthesized from Economics Explained, Predictive History, Warographics.

item.title: Own Your Intelligence: The Quiet Revolution in How We Work with AI
item.description: Everyone is watching the sky for AGI, but the god is already in the room—it's your agent, running on your context, doing your work. The shift from renting frontier AI to owning your own context and tools—your personal library, skills, and infrastructure—is the real leverage, not the raw model weights. Synthesized from IBM Technology, Matt Pocock, Y Combinator.

item.title: Own Your Intelligence: The Diffusion of AGI and the Skills You Keep
item.description: Everyone is watching the sky, but the thing they're watching for is already in the room — a folder of markdown files and a job that finishes while you sleep. The most valuable AI asset is not the model but the personal context and skills you build around it — the 'library and librarian' — which compounds and can be owned, not rented. Synthesized from IBM Technology, Matt Pocock, Y Combinator.
